episode_thesis: Cohen argues that tariffs will slow US growth to about 1.5% (recession odds about 45%, lowered by the China retreat) while the Fed stays cautious on tariff inflation, so with multiples high the index has little upside and should trade sideways in a range with a higher floor after the policy pivot. His operating advice is to rely on facts first and pattern recognition second, keep the bar higher in a new regime after an easy 2024, lower expectations, and return to a consistent process during slumps; most of the conversation is personal reflection with no market content.

worldview_premises.premise: Equity returns depend on growth and on the multiple paid for it; slowing growth with already high multiples leaves little upside for the index.
worldview_premises.support: Repeated assertion ('I'll say it again'); no data shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs are a growth shock that is close to unavoidable and the Fed will not offset it quickly because tariff inflation keeps it worried.
worldview_premises.support: Adding up the 10% baseline, sectoral tariffs and China to a 14-17% effective rate; Fed reaction function assumed.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are not required to rise every year; sideways periods are normal in history.
worldview_premises.support: 'When you look back in history'; no specifics.

worldview_premises.premise: A year that was exceptionally easy (2024: multiples rose, everything worked) is followed by a different regime in which what worked before does not work.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of his PMs' behaviour and results.

worldview_premises.premise: The market's reaction to bad data reveals whether prices already discount slower growth.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning only: if markets hold up on weak data, 'wow, what's going on'.

worldview_premises.premise: Policy-driven shocks can reverse quickly; a policy retreat raises the floor under equities without removing the growth slowdown.
worldview_premises.support: The April 2025 drop and rebound; only the pandemic is a comparable precedent.

worldview_premises.premise: Experience gives pattern recognition: episodes rhyme without being identical.
Good processes still produce bad stretches (baseball slumps), so results over short spans do not prove a process wrong.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy to his baseball players going 0 for 20 while hitting the ball hard.

decision_process.practice: In noisy markets trust analysis of facts (or perceived facts) first, then pattern recognition from past episodes.
decision_process.why: Episodes rhyme but are not identical.

decision_process.practice: Raise the bar for positions in a harder regime; be careful with data-dependent and tariff-affected names that have rallied.
decision_process.why: Not everything works when multiples are high and growth slows.

decision_process.practice: On the index side be somewhat more conservative given a sideways market; sectors differ.
decision_process.why: Slowing growth plus high multiples gives little upside.

decision_process.practice: Watch how the market reacts when the data turns down to judge whether prices are right.
decision_process.why: Reaction to bad news shows what is discounted.

decision_process.practice: During losing stretches return to the process and check you are following it; do not judge it on short runs.
Lower return expectations after an extraordinary year and keep learning rather than stopping at a money target; reduce outside stress.
decision_process.why: Harder environment; adaptation sustains performance; stress compounds.

speakers.evidence_style: Experience and judgement: 47-48 years of trading, analogies (baseball slumps, pandemic as the closest rebound), house probabilities (45% recession) given without a stated model; no backtests or data.

current_views.view: Not in a recession yet; about 45% chance of recession (somewhat lessened by the recent China retreat), with significant growth slowing in any case.
current_views.reasoning: Tariffs add up to a 14-17% effective rate.

current_views.view: Growth of about 1.5% or lower next year (2026) and the Fed will not act right away because of tariff inflation.
current_views.reasoning: Tariff drag and Fed worry about inflation.

current_views.view: Equity market in a trading range for a while with a higher floor; worst case about a 10-15% retrace toward the April lows; little index upside with elevated multiples.
current_views.reasoning: Policy pivot raises the floor; multiples already high with slowing growth.

current_views.view: Be careful with rallied data-dependent and tariff-affected names; wait to see how the market reacts when data turns down.

current_views.reasoning: One-line quick-hit answer with no reasoning.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: He says a decline is not expected yet the market 'feels toppy'; the sideways call and the 10-15% retest possibility are not reconciled with a toppy label.
Recession probability of 45% is given without a method; it was formed before the China retreat and he says odds have 'lessened' without a new number.
He wants to see how the market reacts to bad data to learn whether it is priced correctly, but gives no threshold for what reaction would change his view.
He says analysis first, pattern recognition second, but names no specific analyses, indicators or past episodes beyond the pandemic rebound analogy.
Size of the 2024 outperformance is caption-garbled ('50 75% their normal average': above or below normal).

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Effective US tariff rate (14-17%), incoming growth data (when it turns down), Fed reaction to tariff inflation, index multiples relative to slowing growth, and the market's reaction to weak data; horizon months to the rest of 2025 and into 2026.
reader_inferences: (reader) Cohen's valuation logic treats the multiple as the swing factor: with earnings growth slowing, index upside needs multiple expansion, which he does not expect.
(reader) Roughly four fifths of the interview is life and mentoring content; the market framework rests on only a few minutes of statements.
(reader) 'Raises the floor' implies he reads the policy pivot as a put-like reduction in tail risk rather than a change in the growth path.
